title: Noise-robust discrimination of incoherent point sources with spatial-mode demultiplexing
authors: Jian-Qiang Liu, Chao-Ning Hu, Jun Xin, Xiao-Ming Lu
abstract: We theoretically predict and experimentally demonstrate that a reduced spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) measurement using only the two lowest-order Hermite-Gaussian modes exhibits remarkable robustness against background noise in discriminating between a single source and two incoherent point sources. We establish a theoretical framework incorporating uniform background noise and derive an analytical Chernoff exponent expression, showing that SPADE consistently outperforms direct imaging (DI) across all source separations. Experimental results confirm that SPADE-based hypothesis testing approaches the quantum limit even when the background-to-signal photon ratio per pixel is 0.11. This advantage stems from SPADE's ability to concentrate source information into minimal detection modes, reducing the cumulative background noise impact. Our findings provide a practical detection scheme for applications where background noise is inevitable, such as astronomical observations and quantum sensing.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical and experimental method for distinguishing between one or two closely spaced incoherent light sources in noisy environments. By employing reduced Spatial-Mode Demultiplexing (SPADE), the measurement concentrates source information into specific spatial modes. This technique significantly enhances noise robustness, allowing detection performance to approach the quantum limit even when significant background noise is present.
main_problem: The core problem is discriminating between a single incoherent point source and two closely spaced incoherent point sources when background noise is present, especially in regimes where diffraction causes signal overlap.
main_result: Reduced Spatial-Mode Demultiplexing (SPADE) measurements are theoretically predicted and experimentally shown to be robust against background noise, consistently outperforming direct imaging methods by concentrating source information into minimal detection modes.
method: The authors employ quantum hypothesis testing using the Chernoff exponent ($\xi$) derived from Poisson statistics for photon counts in the weak-source limit. They compare this theoretical bound against Direct Imaging (DI) measurements.
model_or_system: The system involves optical imaging of incoherent point sources, modeled using quantum detection theory and characterized by Hermite-Gaussian (HG) spatial modes. The noise is assumed to be uniform and Poissonian background light.
key_observables: Chernoff exponent ($\xi_{	ext{meas}}$ or $\zeta$), which quantifies the exponential decay rate of the error probability, and the comparison between SPADE vs. DI performance.
important_parameters: Background-to-signal photon ratio (e.g., 0.11), source separation ($d$), and the number of lowest-order HG modes used for measurement.
main_assumptions: The background noise is assumed to be uniform and Poissonian, and the PSF is approximated by a Gaussian function in the weak-source limit.

paper_structure: The paper establishes a theoretical framework using quantum state analysis and Chernoff bounds. It derives the optimal measurement strategy (SPADE) and compares its achievable exponent against direct imaging, culminating in experimental validation showing noise robustness.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it provides a concrete, quantifiable advantage of using structured measurements (spatial modes) over simple intensity measurements when background noise corrupts the signal, pushing detection towards fundamental quantum limits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Numerical results for the quantum Chernoff exponent (red solid line) and the classical Chernoff exponents for SPADE (blue dashed line) and DI (yellow dash-dotted line) with excess noise. The PSF is Gaussian with the standard deviation 𝜎= 115 𝜇m. The DI is set to 1000 pixels with a pixel size 𝑎= 4.6 𝜇m. For SPADE, only the two lowest-order HG modes are included in the calculation of the Chernoff exponent.

Fig. 3. Experimental setup for the SPADE-based hypothesis testing. DMD, digital micromirror device; CGH, computer-generated hologram; SLM, spatial light modulator. Only the first-order diffraction from the SLM is directed to the CMOS camera.

Fig. 4. Error probability and Chernoff exponent of SPADE-based hypothesis testing. The noise-to-signal ratio in this experiment is 𝑏/𝜈≈0.11. The first four panels show the error probability 𝑃err of SPADE as a function of 𝜈for the separations 𝑑1 = 0.67𝜎, 𝑑2 = 1.01𝜎, 𝑑3 = 1.35𝜎, and 𝑑4 = 1.68𝜎, respectively. The solid lines are fits to 𝑃err ∝exp(−𝜈𝜉P), with 𝜉P the extracted Chernoff exponent. The bottom panel shows the extracted Chernoff exponent 𝜉P as a function of the separation 𝑑.
